opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about for a long time. Tokenization is one of those things everyone treats as a fixed preprocessing step, but it's really a handcrafted heuristic sitting at the front of the pipeline. BPE and similar methods compress text into chunks that are roughly meaningful, and that works well enough for English, but you see the cracks quickly: other languages, code, numbers, character-level tasks like spelling or counting letters, and especially modalities like DNA or audio where there's no obvious notion of a "word."

So the question I keep coming back to is: why can't the model learn its own units of abstraction? Deep learning's whole story has been replacing handcrafted features with learned ones, and tokenization is one of the last big holdouts.

The difficulty is that working directly on raw bytes or raw signals makes sequences much longer, and with standard attention, which scales quadratically, that gets expensive fast. That's part of what drew me to state space models and architectures like Mamba. They process long sequences efficiently, and they behave a lot like compressors: they maintain a state that summarizes what came before. That's a natural fit for fine-grained, raw data.

But efficiency alone isn't enough. Even with a linear-time model, you don't want to spend the same compute on every byte. Some parts of the input carry much more information than others. What you really want is hierarchy: the model processes low-level units, decides on its own where the meaningful boundaries are, groups things into higher-level chunks, and does its heavier reasoning at that coarser level. That's the idea behind dynamic chunking. You learn the segmentation end to end instead of fixing it beforehand.

What's exciting is that when you do this, the model starts discovering boundaries that look somewhat like words or morphemes on its own, and it can adapt to the data. On text without clean whitespace, or code, or genomic sequences, the learned approach tends to help more, precisely because the hand-designed tokenizer was a poor fit there.

More broadly, I think of it as removing one of the strongest inductive biases we've baked in without really questioning it. If we want models that learn from the messy, unstructured data of the world, including audio, video, sensor streams, and biology, we can't hand-design a tokenizer for each one. The model has to learn how to compress and abstract its input itself. There's still a lot of work to do on making training stable, scaling it, and getting the hierarchy deeper, but I think that's the direction things will go.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization compresses text into chunks and contrasts this with raw byte sequences, which are much longer and costly under quadratic attention. This communicates tokenization’s computational efficiency benefit.

r002.rationale: It describes sequence length and attention cost as constraints, but does not frame imposed structure in machine learning as a response to technological constraints.

r003.rationale: It presents replacing handcrafted features with learned abstractions as a direction in deep learning, but does not connect that reduction in imposed structure to improving available capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, and I think it's one of the more important directions for the field. Tokenization has always bothered me, honestly. If you step back and look at the whole deep learning story, the trend has been to remove hand-engineered pipelines and let the model learn end to end from raw data. We did that with features in vision, we did that with a lot of the structure in speech. But in language, we still have this tokenizer sitting at the front of the model that was built with heuristics like byte pair encoding, and it's kind of this last vestige of a hand-designed preprocessing step.

And it causes real problems. It's brittle on things like spelling and character-level tasks, it behaves poorly across languages and scripts, it's bad on code and on noisy text, and it makes the model worse at certain kinds of reasoning that depend on what's actually inside a word. Beyond the practical issues, I think it's a sign that the architecture isn't doing something it should be doing, which is figuring out the right units of abstraction on its own.

The reason we haven't gotten rid of it is mostly that Transformers don't work well on raw bytes. Attention is quadratic, and if you blow up your sequence length by four or five times by going to bytes, that's expensive. But more fundamentally, Transformers kind of need the data to be pre-compressed into meaningful units. Tokenization is doing a lot of work for them, and when you take it away, performance drops. State space models, like what we did with Mamba, behave differently here. Because they compress the history into a fixed-size state, they're more naturally suited to high-resolution data where the individual elements don't carry much information. That's one of the things that pushed me toward this question.

The way I think about the actual solution is hierarchy. Instead of a fixed tokenizer, you want the model to learn its own segmentation, to decide dynamically where the boundaries are and to operate at multiple levels of resolution. At the low level you process raw bytes, and then the model learns to chunk those into higher-level units, and the heavy computation happens on those compressed representations. The key is that the chunking has to be learned and data-dependent, not a fixed rule, and it has to be differentiable so you can train the whole thing end to end. That's hard to get right. You need the right architectural design and the right training signals so the model doesn't collapse to trivial segmentations. But when it works, you see the model discover things that look like words and subwords on its own, and it tends to scale better and generalize more robustly than a tokenized baseline.

What's really exciting to me is that this isn't just about language. Once you can learn from raw bytes, the same machinery should apply to any modality. Language is actually the easy case because it's already been compressed by humans into a pretty structured form. DNA, audio, video, sensor data, all of that is much more raw and much longer, and that's where I think learned hierarchical approaches have a big advantage. So I see moving beyond tokenization as the first step toward architectures that can find structure in any kind of data, which is really what I think the end goal of this field should be.

r001.rationale: It says byte-level sequences are four or five times longer and make quadratic attention expensive, and that tokenization pre-compresses the data for Transformers.

r002.rationale: It links the continued use of tokenization to Transformer limits: raw-byte sequences are expensive and Transformers perform poorly without pre-compressed units.

r003.rationale: It describes deep learning’s trend as removing hand-engineered pipelines and presents learned, hierarchical processing as a way to move beyond fixed tokenization.

astra-6.text:
I think tokenization is a useful practical tool, but it’s also a choice we impose on the model before it gets to learn anything. We decide what the basic units should be, and that affects both what the model can represent and how efficiently it can process the data.

What I find exciting is the possibility of moving some of that choice into the model itself. For text, you could start with bytes; for audio, you could start with the waveform. Then the question is whether the model can learn useful structure at different scales, instead of us specifying those scales ahead of time.

The challenge is that those raw sequences can be much longer. A model has to process a lot of local detail while still capturing relationships over long distances. That’s one motivation for working on efficient sequence models: you want the cost of processing the input to be low enough that you can actually explore this direction.

But efficiency alone doesn’t solve it. Ideally, the model would also learn when to compress information and when to preserve detail. To me, that’s a really interesting research question: can we learn the representations and the computational structure together, directly from the data?

r001.rationale: It says tokenization affects efficiency, but does not state that tokenization substantially improves computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It describes tokenization as an imposed choice and mentions efficiency, but does not frame imposed structure as a response to technological constraints.

r003.rationale: It considers learning representations directly from data, but does not connect reducing imposed structure to improving available capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how much structure we want to impose before the model ever sees the data. Tokenization is one way of doing that: we choose a representation, and then the model learns over that representation. It’s useful, but it also introduces assumptions about what the meaningful units are.

If you want to learn more directly from something like audio or a stream of bytes, the sequences can become much longer. So the modeling challenge is partly computational: can you process all of that efficiently? But it’s also about learning abstractions. Can the model figure out which local details matter, how to combine them, and what information to retain over longer timescales?

That’s one of the motivations for working on efficient sequence models. Ideally, you’d give the model more freedom to discover the right representation instead of fixing it all in preprocessing. But removing tokenization doesn’t remove the problem of representation—it moves more of that problem into the model.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization chooses a representation and notes that direct learning can create computational challenges, but it does not say tokenization substantially improves computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It discusses imposed structure and computational constraints separately, without framing imposed structure as a response to technological constraints.

r003.rationale: It expresses a preference for giving models more freedom, but does not describe progress reducing imposed structure as capabilities improve.
